Testimony in Support: LD 2078, An Act to Establish the Electricity Cost Fairness Refundable Tax Credit
Greetings Senator Grohoski, Representative Sayre, and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation. My name is Alf Anderson, and I am an Associate State Director for Advocacy and Outreach for AARP Maine. AARP is a non-profit, non-partisan social mission organization with more than 200,000 members across the state. We work on a range of issues at the state level that are of importance to Mainers 50 and older.
I am submitting this testimony in Support of LD 2078 because it would be a step in the right direction in addressing the affordability challenges being faced by so many electricity ratepayers today.
The proposed Electricity Cost Fairness Credit aligns directly with our organization's mission to promote economic equity and reduce the burden of essential utility costs on Maine households. By targeting relief to those most affected by high electricity costs and indexing the benefit to inflation, the legislation aims to ensure ongoing relevance and effectiveness in addressing cost-of-living challenges.
The bill's structure, including its phase-out provisions and refundability, is designed to maximize impact for lower- and moderate-income families, which aligns with the AARP's focus on supporting vulnerable populations.
We would also highlight for the committee that there are many older Mainers who are not required to file tax returns and may not benefit from this program as currently proposed. We would recommend the consideration of an amendment that could address this group, who are also facing affordability challenges.
Late in 2024, AARP conducted a survey of Mainers over the age of 45. According to those results, 80% of respondents felt that legislators were not doing enough to keep electricity affordable. We see LD 2078 as creative legislative action to begin addressing the concerns of those on low- and fixed-incomes and we urge the committee members to vote in favor of the bill.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide our views on this important bill. If I can answer any questions or provide any further information, you can reach me at aanderson@aarp.org or 207.330.1147. Alf Anderson Associate State Director, Advocacy and Outreach AARP Maine

Karen Blakelock, Policy Advisor The Nature Conservancy in Maine karen.blakelock@tnc.org
Joint Standing Committee on Taxation
RE: LD 2078--An Act to Establish the Electricity Cost Fairness Refundable Tax Credit
Senator Grohoski, Representative Sayre, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation my name is Karen Blakelock, and I work as the energy policy advisor for the Nature Conservancy in Maine. I appreciate this opportunity to comment in support of LD 2078.
The Nature Conservancy (TNC) is a nonprofit conservation organization dedicated to conserving the lands and waters on which all life depends. Guided by science, we create innovative, on-theground solutions to our world's toughest challenges so that both nature and people can thrive. We work in more than 70 countries, and use a collaborative approach that engages local communities, governments, the private sector, and other partners.
In November 2025, the Office of the Public Advocate released a statement that, in the face of rising and volatile energy costs, "affordability must remain at the center of every decision we make about Maine's energy future."1 Polling that TNC conducted last February demonstrated that the vast majority of Mainers view the cost of living and the cost of electricity to be very serious problems. LD 2078 offers a step towards a solution. While we must rapidly transition to an economy powered by clean and renewable energy sources in an increasingly electrified society, it is imperative that we do so in a way that does not leave the most vulnerable members of our communities behind.
For example, while Maine has been a national leader in installing heat pumps and offering rebates for low- and moderate-income customers, unfortunate consequences arise when households are unable to afford their monthly electric bill and hesitate to use their source of electric heat for fear of rising costs. While the price of electricity in New England is largely set by fluctuations in natural gas prices, we do know that heat pumps can help save money over time, reduce health impacts by improving indoor air quality, and help efficiently heat or cool while reducing reliance on fossil fuels. As society at large becomes increasingly dependent on electricity, we must be working towards a future powered by clean and renewable energy that leaves no one behind.
LD 2078 is an innovative approach to solving a problem every state is grappling with. More than a quarter-way through the 21st century, electricity should be accessible to all Mainers, and TNC supports this committee considering ways to ensure that the most vulnerable members of our communities are not left behind.
1 https://www.maine.gov/meopa/about/news/public-advocate-responds-2026-standard-offer-supply-rateincreases

I ask that you vote Ought to Pass on LD 2078. Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments, I am happy to answer any questions now or in the future.

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation

Senator Grohoski, Representative Sayre and distinguished members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Taxation, I am Kilton Webb, and I represent House District 98, which includes
Durham, Pownal, and parts of Lisbon, Bowdoin and Topsham. I am here today to introduce LD 2078, An Act to Establish the Electricity Cost Fairness Refundable Tax Credit.

LD 2078 would provide targeted relief for eligible Mainers through a new income tax credit of
up to $600 per year, putting money directly back into the pockets of those who need it most. The credit would work similar to the state's existing Property Tax Fairness Credit and Sales Tax
Faimess Credit, which are two proven policies that have helped lessen the financial burdens
facing many Mainers.

One of the biggest issues I hear from constituents is that the rising cost of living is making it harder and harder for working families to make ends meet, let alone get ahead. In addition to the
increasing costs of housing, healthcare, groceries and other everyday essentials, the rising cost of energy is creating additional stress and taking more and more out of the pockets of working
Mainers.

Maine has seen significant increases in the cost of electricity in the last two years in particular as a result of the regions dependence on natural gas to produce electricity. Natural gas prices are up
over 30% and that has had a direct impact on the state's electricity rates. The Public Advocate
has stated that Mainers should expect at least a $150 increase in the average electricity bill this
year and that is on top of significant increases last year. On top of that, there are proposals to
increase rates again to pay for infrastructure upgrades. As the cost continues to rise and macroeconomic pressures mount, one thing is clear. Our most vulnerable Mainers are in need of relief, and it is our job to think of and work on creative ways to help them.

Electricity is a necessity, not a luxury. No household should have to choose between paying their electricity bill or buying groceries. Sadly, this is the reality for some of our neighbors. I know this because that was my life growing up. When I was a kid, there were times when things got tight, and my parents had to make those difficult decisions. There were a lot of months when the

House District 98: Durham, Pownal, Lisbon (part), Bowdoin (part), Topsham (part)

phone and internet bill got paid late. While this committee isn't the place to go into specific
policy detail on lowering energy costs, it can be a place where we can make a real difference.
This bill offers a meaningful step forward that will directly help ease the financial burden that countless Mainers are feeling. Using the state's income tax to provide this kind of relief makes good sense and provides an easy
mechanism to give support to those most effected by rising electricity rates. This is not a new concept or policy change; we currently provide relief to student loan borrowers, parents paying
for childcare or adult dependent care, support for parents with young children and low-income workers all through the state income tax code. This is simply an extension of those valuable
programs. By linking this proposal to the income tax, we can continue to provide a simple one form method to provide targeted relief to Mainers who are struggling. There have been attempts, and I know there will be more, to lower energy rates through regulation and ratepayer reform. As a member of the Energy, Utilities and Technology Committee, I can tell you that we will continue to work to lower rates, but those are
longer term projects that will take time to see results. We need relief now, and that relief can best be brought to Maine rate payers by providing this kind of targeted help. We need to be doing
everything we can to ensure that our neighbors, including working families, veterans and seniors
on fixed incomes, can afford to keep their lights on --- literally.
Thank you for your consideration. I am happy to answer any questions you may have about the
bill.
House District 98: Durham, Pownal, Lisbon (pait), Bowdoin (part), Topsham (part)
196554:
TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL J. ALLEN, ASSOCIATE COMMISSIONER FOR TAX POLICY
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation
Hearing Date: January 21", 2026
LD 2078 -- "An Act to Establish the Electricity Cost Fairness Refundable Tax
Credit" _
Senator Grohoski, Representative Sayre, and members of the Taxation
Committee -- good afternoon, my name is Michael Allen, Associate Commissioner for Tax Policy in the Department of Administrative and Financial Services. I am testifying at the request of the Administration Against LD 2078, "An Act to
Establish the Electricity Cost Fairness Refundable Tax Credit."
While laudable in intent, this bill does not solve the underlying issue of high energy costs, and instead further complicates the Maine income tax by creating
another costly and complex refundable tax credit. A complicated tax code burdens
both taxpayers and the State.
For tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, the bill proposes to establish the Electricity Cost Fairness Credit, a refundable credit for Maine residents and part-year residents. The base credit amount ranges from $335 to $600, depending on the taxpayer's filing status and number of dependents claimed for purposes of the federal child tax credit. For part-year residents, the credit is prorated based on Maine-source income.
The credit is phased out for taxpayers Whose income exceeds $20,000 for taxpayers filing single, $30,000 for taxpayers filing as heads of household, and $40,000 for married taxpayers filing jointly. The credit is not available to married

taxpayers filing separate returns, individuals who are "safe harbor" residents
treated as nonresident individuals because they reside outside Maine for significant
periods of time, and individuals that may be claimed as a dependent on another
person's income tax return. The credit's structure is comparable to the Sales Tax Fairness Credit ("STFC") and is adjusted for inflation annually beginning in 2027.
For tax year 2025, the refundable STFC, as adjusted for inflation, is a
maximum credit up to $280, depending on the number of qualifying children and
dependents on the Maine income tax return. The income phaseout begins at $25,450 for single filers, $38,200 for heads of households, and $50,950 for married filing jointly or qualifying widow(er). Aside from the technical and legal concerns
listed in the Appendix, the refundable tax credit this bill introduces only differs
from the STFC by the base credit amount and the phaseout range.
As such, a simpler approach for the Committee to consider is increasing the existing STFC instead of creating an additional tax credit. This approach would
also avoid the issue of phasing out multiple credits over similar income tax ranges -- a practice that can create surprisingly high effective marginal tax rates for, in this case, lower income taxpayers.
The Department would also suggest that non-tax solutions may better
address the issue of high electricity costs. Electricity is a regulated market Where other agencies not only have a higher degree of subject matter expertise than Maine Revenue Services, but also have existing authority in the field. Directly addressing electricity costs would be simpler, quicker, and more effective than
involving a new agency and requiring taxpayers to wait until tax filing season to claim a new credit on their tax returns.

The preliminary fiscal impact estimate projects an annual revenue loss of $45 million. The bill's estimated administrative costs are under review. The bill will result in one-time computer programming and related system testing costs to add one additional line to the individual income tax return and four new lines to Schedule PTFC/STFC to accommodate the credit. Due to lack of available space on the current Schedule PTFC/STFC, additional printing and associated mailing
costs will be incurred to add another page to the Schedule.
Appendix:
0 The credit first applies to tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026; however, the first inflation adjustments are required to be made in 2027. Therefore, the base credit and the income phaseout thresholds will not be adjusted until tax years beginning on or after
January 1, 2028.
0 Unlike the STFC, the federal deduction for alimony paid is not considered income for purposes of determining the credit.
0 Restricting the credit to Maine residents may raise concenis under the United States
Constitution. Further research is required.
0 Adding another refundable credit may increase the risk of fraudulent claims.

Testimony of Rep. Sally Cluchey in support of LD 2078, An Act to Establish the Electricity Cost Fairness Refundable Tax
Credit Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation
Senator Grohoski, Representative Sayre, and distinguished members of the Taxation Committee, my name is Sally Cluchey, and I represent House District 52, which includes Bowdoinham, Richmond, and part of Bowdoin. I am here today to support LD 2078, An Act to Establish the Electricity Cost Fairness Refundable Tax Credit.
Electricity is not a luxury -- it's a necessity. Yet rising electricity costs are forcing too many Maine families to make impossible choices: do they pay the electric bill or buy groceries? Do they heat their homes or fill their prescriptions? These aren't theoretical scenarios. I've heard these stories directly from constituents in my district, and I know you've heard them in yours.
While the Legislature cannot control the market forces driving energy costs, we can provide meaningful relief to those bearing the heaviest burden. LD 2078 offers a practical, targeted solution: an income tax credit of up to $600 per year for eligible Mainers, putting money directly back into the pockets of those who need it most.
This approach is not experimental -- it builds on the proven success of our Property Tax Fairness Credit and Sales Tax Fairness Credit, policies that have already helped thousands of Maine families manage their cost of living. The Electricity Cost Fairness Credit would extend that same principle to another essential expense.
Working families shouldn't have to choose between keeping their lights on and meeting other basic needs. We have an opportunity -- and I would argue a responsibility -- to provide this relief. I urge you to support LD 2078.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

District 52: Bowdoin (part), Bowdoinham and Richmond
